meta.title: Excitable Tissues
meta.summary: Every cell has a voltage across its membrane. Excitable cells are the ones that can suddenly flip it — and that flip is a signal.

Resting Membrane Potential — The Charged Calm Before the Storm
The Action Potential — The Nerve Impulse Itself
How Fast Does the Signal Travel?

items: Every cell has a voltage across its membrane. Excitable cells are the ones that can suddenly flip it — and that flip is a signal.
Topic 01 charged the battery with the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. This topic spends it.
The nerve impulse is not electricity flowing along a wire like a cable. It is a chain reaction travelling along the membrane — closer to a line of dominoes, or a burning fuse, than to a copper wire.
Get three ideas and the rest follows: a resting voltage, a threshold, and all-or-none firing.
Excitable tissue = tissue that responds to a stimulus with a rapid change in membrane potential — nerve, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and some gland cells.
The requirement is simple: a charge difference across the membrane, and gates that can open fast.
Everything else in this topic is just the detail of how that flip happens, how fast it travels, and how it is turned into a sensation.

blocks.x: Most cells just quietly do their metabolic business. But a special group of cells can do something dramatic: they can generate a tiny electrical spark, on command, and send that spark racing along their length. That's excitability — and it's the basis of literally everything you think, feel, and move.

blocks.name: Excitable tissues (definition)
blocks.def: Tissues capable of producing electrical signals when excited. Excitability of cells and tissues is a basic function of life. The three excitable tissues are: nerves, muscles, and sensory receptors.

sections.title: The Neuron — Anatomy of a Signal-Carrier

items: A neuron is built like a messaging office: dendrites are the inbox (collecting signals), the soma is the desk where they are added up, the axon is the outgoing cable, and the terminals are the outbox that pass the message on.
Myelin is insulation. It is not there to carry the signal — it is there to stop it leaking, so the impulse can jump ahead instead of crawling.
Two cell populations exist in the nervous system: neurons (which signal) and glia (which support). Glia vastly outnumber neurons.
Neurons are long-lived and largely irreplaceable — which is why nerve damage is so serious compared with, say, a cut in the skin.
Multiple sclerosis is essentially insulation stripping off the wiring — the neuron survives, but signals leak, slow and misfire.
A trapped nerve going numb and 'pins-and-needles' is signalling being disrupted along the cable, not the muscle failing.

blocks.cap: The parts of a neuron and the direction a signal travels through them.

blocks.name: The nervous system's two cell populations
blocks.def: Neurons and glial cells. Glial cells actually make up about half of the total volume of the brain and spinal cord — they're not a minor supporting cast, they're roughly half the tissue.

blocks.name: Neurons
blocks.def: Also called neurones or nerve cells — electrically excitable cells in the nervous system that process and transmit information. A typical neuron has all the usual cell parts PLUS specialized structures: the soma, dendrites, and axon.

blocks.name: Soma (cell body)
blocks.def: The metabolic center of the neuron. Contains the nucleus, which contains the genetic material (chromosomes).

blocks.name: Dendrites
blocks.def: Extensions from the soma that often look like branches or spikes, tapering toward their tips. Their surfaces RECEIVE chemical messages from other neurons — dendrites are the 'listening' end of the cell.

blocks.name: Axon
blocks.def: A long, slender extension from the soma that emerges at a specific point called the axon hillock. It has a uniform diameter and conducts electrical impulses AWAY from the soma — the axon is the 'transmitting' end of the cell.

blocks.name: Telodendria (terminal buttons / synaptic end bulbs)
blocks.def: The distal (far) endings of an axon, specialized for releasing neurotransmitters onto the next cell.

blocks.name: Myelinated vs unmyelinated axons
blocks.def: Myelinated neurons have a neurilemma or sheath of glial cells wrapped tightly around the axon, forming the myelin sheath. Unmyelinated neurons lack this wrapping — their glial cells simply form a groove or valley that the axon sits in, without wrapping around it.

items: By job: sensory (afferent) carry information in toward the CNS; motor (efferent) carry commands out; interneurons sit between them and do the processing.
A memory hook that works: Afferent = Arriving, Efferent = Exiting.
By shape: unipolar (mostly sensory), bipolar (special senses such as retina and smell), multipolar (the commonest — most motor neurons and interneurons).
Interneurons are the overwhelming majority in the CNS — most of your nervous system is neither sensing nor acting, it is deciding.
Touching a hot pot: sensory neurons carry 'hot!' in, interneurons in the spinal cord decide instantly, motor neurons pull the hand away — and you feel the pain only after your hand has already moved.

blocks.x: Neurons can be sorted three different ways — by which direction they carry signals, by how many processes stick out of them, and by which chemical they release. Same neuron, three different labels depending on which question you're asking.

blocks.name: Functional classification of neurons (overview)
blocks.def: Based on the direction of nerve impulse travel relative to the CNS. Three categories: sensory/afferent, motor/efferent, and interneurons.

blocks.name: Sensory (afferent) neurons
blocks.def: Convey information FROM tissues and organs TO the central nervous system — carrying signals inward, toward the CNS.

blocks.name: Motor (efferent) neurons
blocks.def: Transmit signals FROM the central nervous system TO effector cells (muscles, glands) — carrying signals outward, away from the CNS. Has two branches: the somatic system, and the autonomic system (itself subdivided into sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions).

blocks.name: Interneurons
blocks.def: Neurons that provide connections between sensory and motor neurons, and between each other. Crucially, ALL of the neurons of the central nervous system (including the brain) are interneurons — the brain itself is essentially a vast network of interneurons doing the connecting and processing.

blocks.name: Structural classification of neurons (overview)
blocks.def: Based on the number of processes extending off the cell body. Three classes: unipolar (pseudounipolar), bipolar, and multipolar.

blocks.name: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons
blocks.def: Have one short process that immediately splits into two very long processes, both of which function as axons. Common, and found primarily in the afferent (sensory) division of the PNS.

blocks.name: Bipolar neurons
blocks.def: Consist of a single axon and a single dendrite (two processes total). Rare — found in the retina of the eye, olfactory epithelium cells, and several cranial nerves.

blocks.name: Multipolar neurons
blocks.def: Have MULTIPLE dendritic processes, giving them an irregular shape, but each neuron still has only ONE axon. The most common type, comprising more than 99% of neurons in humans — the major neuron type found in the CNS and the efferent (motor) division of the PNS.

blocks.name: Classification of neurons by <term d="A chemical messenger released by a nerve cell to pass a signal across a synapse.">neurotransmitter</term> released
blocks.def: Neurons can also be classified chemically, by which neurotransmitter(s) they release: cholinergic, adrenergic, peptidergic, purinergic, and nonadrenergic-noncholinergic neurons.

items: Neurons get the glory; glia keep them alive. Think pit crew, not driver.
Astrocytes — housekeeping: they support the blood–brain barrier, control the chemical environment and mop up excess transmitter.
Oligodendrocytes (in the CNS) and Schwann cells (in the PNS) — the insulation crew that make myelin.
Microglia — the immune squad; they clean up damage and debris.
Ependymal cells — line the cavities and help make and circulate cerebrospinal fluid.
Satellite cells — surround and support neuron cell bodies in ganglia.
The blood–brain barrier that astrocytes help maintain is why many drugs simply cannot reach the brain — and why the few that do (alcohol, caffeine, anaesthetics) act so powerfully.

blocks.name: Glial cells (general functions)
blocks.def: Provide support and protection for neurons. Four main functions: surround neurons and hold them in place, supply nutrients and oxygen to neurons, insulate one neuron from another, and destroy/remove the carcasses of dead neurons (clean-up duty).

blocks.name: Astrocytes
blocks.def: Give nutritional support to the CNS, provide a supportive 'skeleton,' and are essential in forming and maintaining the blood-brain barrier. They also help maintain an appropriate chemical environment for neuronal signaling in various ways.

blocks.name: Oligodendrocytes
blocks.def: Form the myelin sheath around axons of the CNS, and help hold nerve fibers together.

blocks.name: Microglia
blocks.def: Phagocyte cells that migrate through the CNS, removing foreign matter and degenerated brain tissue — the CNS's clean-up crew and immune defense.

blocks.name: Ependymal cells
blocks.def: Epithelial cells that line the ventricles of the brain and the spinal cord; they form cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and help circulate it.

blocks.name: Schwann cells
blocks.def: The PNS supporting cell that forms myelin sheaths around peripheral axons.

blocks.name: Satellite cells
blocks.def: The PNS supporting cell that encapsulates and provides protection and support for the cell bodies of peripheral neurons.

sections.title: Resting Membrane Potential — The Charged Calm Before the Storm

items: At rest the inside of the cell is negative relative to the outside — about −70 mV in a typical neuron. The cell is said to be polarized.
Two things create it: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (which builds the gradients) and, more importantly for the voltage itself, K⁺ leak channels that let potassium drift out, leaving negativity behind.
The equilibrium potential of an ion is the voltage at which its urge to move down its concentration gradient is exactly balanced by the electrical pull. The Nernst equation calculates it for one ion.
The real resting potential sits close to EK⁺ but slightly less negative, because the membrane is not perfectly K⁺-selective — a small amount of Na⁺ leaks in.
The GHK equation is simply the honest version: it accounts for several ions at once, weighted by how permeable the membrane is to each.
The practical takeaway: the resting potential is dominated by K⁺. Change extracellular K⁺ and you move the resting potential — which is why potassium is monitored so anxiously in hospital.
A charged phone sitting on the table doing nothing is the perfect image: potential energy stored, ready to be spent the instant it is needed.

Potassium abnormalities are dangerous precisely because the heart is an excitable tissue — shifting resting potential can stop it. This is why potassium is one of the most closely watched numbers in medicine.

blocks.x: Even when a neuron is doing 'nothing,' it isn't electrically neutral — it's sitting there like a tiny charged battery, with the inside more negative than the outside. This standing voltage is the resting membrane potential, and it's the platform every electrical signal launches from.

blocks.name: Membrane potential (definition)
blocks.def: The electrical potential difference (voltage) across a cell's <term d="The straw-coloured liquid part of blood that carries the cells, proteins, nutrients and wastes.">plasma</term> membrane, resulting from a separation of charges across that membrane. The potential difference across a RESTING cell specifically is called the resting membrane potential.

blocks.name: Scale of the charges involved
blocks.def: Only an insignificant fraction of the total charged particles present in body fluids is actually responsible for generating the membrane potential — you don't need to move much charge to create a meaningful voltage difference.

blocks.name: Polarized cell
blocks.def: A resting cell is described as 'polarized' because the resting potential has a negative value — by convention, this means there is excess negative charge INSIDE the cell compared to outside. The magnitude typically ranges from about -9 mV to -100 mV depending on cell type.

blocks.name: Three factors that determine membrane potential
blocks.def: The unequal distribution of K+, Na+, Cl-, and large intracellular anions across the membrane; the permeability of the membrane to those ions (ion conductance, via specific channels); and the activity of electrogenic pumps (like Na+/K+-ATPase and Ca2+ transport pumps) that maintain those concentration gradients.

blocks.name: The two proteins mainly responsible for the RMP
blocks.def: A K+ leak channel, responsible for about 80% of the resting potential's basis (the resting membrane is 50-75 times MORE permeable to K+ than to Na+, making K+ movement the prime determinant of RMP); and the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, responsible for about 20%, both directly (it's electrogenic, since it pumps 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in, a net charge movement) and indirectly (by creating and maintaining the concentration gradients that the leak channels then exploit).

blocks.name: Equilibrium potential
blocks.def: For a specific ion, the membrane potential at which there is NO net movement of that ion across the membrane — the point where the electrical pull and the concentration-driven pull on that ion exactly balance out.

blocks.name: The Nernst equation
blocks.def: The equation used to calculate the equilibrium potential for a single specific ion, based on the ion's concentration inside vs outside the cell, its valence (charge), and temperature.

blocks.name: Key equilibrium potential values to know
blocks.def: EK+ (potassium) ≈ -90 mV; ENa+ (sodium) ≈ +60 mV; ECl- (chloride) ≈ -70 mV. Compare these to the actual measured resting membrane potential of a neuron, about -70 mV — notice it sits very close to EK+, confirming K+ is the dominant influence.

blocks.name: Why the actual RMP is slightly less negative than EK+
blocks.def: A small number of Na+ ions constantly leak into the cell, nudging the resting potential slightly positive of the pure potassium equilibrium potential — the RMP is a compromise, dominated by K+ but slightly pulled toward Na+.

blocks.name: The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz (GHK) equation
blocks.def: Used to calculate the resting membrane potential when SEVERAL different ions and their differing permeabilities must be accounted for simultaneously (unlike the Nernst equation, which handles only one ion at a time).

blocks.name: Effect of changing extracellular K+ and Na+ on RMP
blocks.def: Increasing external K+ concentration DECREASES the resting membrane potential (makes it less negative) — because K+ so strongly dominates RMP. Decreasing external Na+ concentration has comparatively LITTLE effect on RMP, since Na+ plays only a minor role at rest.

sections.title: The Action Potential — The Nerve Impulse Itself

items: Two kinds of electrical response: graded potentials (small, local, variable in size, they fade with distance) and action potentials (large, self-regenerating, they travel the whole length without shrinking).
All-or-none: if the stimulus reaches threshold you get a full-sized spike; if it does not, you get nothing. There is no half an action potential.

The sequence: threshold reached → Na⁺ gates fly open → Na⁺ floods in → inside goes positive (depolarization) → Na⁺ gates shut and K⁺ gates open → K⁺ leaves → voltage falls back (repolarization) → a brief overshoot (after-hyperpolarization) → back to rest.
It propagates because each patch of membrane depolarizes the patch next door past threshold — a chain reaction, not a current flowing down a wire.
Because the spike is always the same size, intensity cannot be coded by size. A strong stimulus is signalled by firing more often, and by recruiting more fibres.
A toilet flush: press lightly and nothing happens; press past a point and you get the whole flush, every time, the same size — you cannot flush harder.
Dominoes: the last domino falls just as hard as the first, because each one supplies its own energy — that is why the impulse does not fade over a metre of nerve.
A light touch versus a hard pinch feel different not because the spikes are bigger, but because they arrive faster and from more fibres.

blocks.x: If resting potential is the calm battery charge, the action potential is the lightning bolt. It's an all-or-nothing electrical event that, once triggered, races down the axon exactly the same way every single time — like flipping a light switch rather than turning a dimmer.

blocks.name: Two types of electrical response to stimulation
blocks.def: Graded (local/electrotonic/generator) potentials, and action potentials. Which one you get depends on the intensity of the stimulation.

blocks.name: Graded potentials
blocks.def: A NON-propagating, localized potential difference across the neuron's membrane, elicited by a stimulus of SUBTHRESHOLD strength. It declines with time and distance from the stimulus point, arises mainly in dendrites and cell bodies, shows no reversal of polarity, has an amplitude that depends on stimulus strength (ranging from under 1 mV to over 50 mV), has a longer duration (msec to several minutes), may be hyperpolarizing (inhibitory) or depolarizing (excitatory), has NO <term d="A short spell straight after firing when the cell cannot fire again, or needs a stronger stimulus.">refractory period</term>, and shows temporal and spatial summation.

blocks.name: Action potential (definition)
blocks.def: A self-propagating electrical potential difference produced across the plasma membrane of nerve or muscle cells when stimulated. Initiated only by a stimulus ABOVE a certain intensity (<term d="The minimum strength of stimulus needed to trigger an action potential.">threshold</term>); shows a transient REVERSAL of polarity; arises at trigger zones and propagates along the axon; is 'all or none,' typically about 100 mV in size; has a shorter duration (0.5-2 msec); always consists of a depolarizing phase followed by repolarization and return to RMP; HAS a refractory period; and is NOT subject to summation.

blocks.x: ▶️Generation of Action PotentialVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: All-or-none principle
blocks.def: An action potential either happens fully, at a fixed size, or doesn't happen at all — there's no such thing as a 'partial' action potential, unlike graded potentials, which scale with stimulus strength.

blocks.name: Four phases of the action potential
blocks.def: Latent period, depolarization, repolarization, and after-hyperpolarization — in that order, on every single action potential.

blocks.name: Latent period
blocks.def: The isoelectric interval — the time taken for the stimulus to travel from the point of stimulation to the recording electrode, before any voltage change is seen.

blocks.name: Depolarization phase
blocks.def: A depolarization of adequate rate and magnitude causes voltage-gated Na+ channels to open, making the membrane 4,000-5,000-fold MORE permeable to Na+, driving the interior potential from -70 mV up toward -55 mV. Once this action threshold is reached, MORE voltage-gated Na+ channels open via a <term d="A loop where the response amplifies the original change, pushing it further until an end point is reached.">positive feedback</term> loop, and the resulting Na+ influx drives the interior of the membrane up to about +40 mV. Voltage-gated K+ channels also begin opening at this point, but much more slowly, giving depolarization time to complete before repolarization kicks in.

blocks.name: Repolarization phase
blocks.def: Na+ channels show rapid inactivation, sharply decreasing Na+ conductance even before they fully close; the now-positive interior repels further Na+ influx; and the PROLONGED opening of voltage-gated K+ channels increases K+ conductance, driving the potential back down toward resting level.

blocks.name: After-hyperpolarization
blocks.def: With both voltage-gated AND non-gated K+ channels open at once, the membrane potential briefly becomes MORE negative than the normal resting potential. Resting potential is regained through closure of the voltage-gated K+ channels, continued K+ efflux through non-gated channels, and restoration of resting ion concentrations by the Na+-K+ pump. Note: decreasing external Na+ concentration decreases the SIZE of the action potential, since Na+ influx is what drives the depolarizing spike.

blocks.name: Propagation of action potentials
blocks.def: Once generated at one site, an AP is conducted along the axon by local current flow. The new action potential's positive charges (inside the cell) spread from the active site toward the negative charges at the adjacent, still-inactive site. This local current causes the adjacent region to depolarize to threshold, generating a fresh action potential there — the process repeats itself down the entire length of the axon, regenerating fully at each segment.

sections.title: How Fast Does the Signal Travel?

items: Three things set the speed: fibre diameter, myelination, and temperature.
Thicker = faster — less internal resistance, like a wide pipe versus a narrow one.
Myelinated = much faster. The impulse leaps from gap to gap (node to node) instead of regenerating at every point — saltatory conduction, from the Latin for 'to jump'.
Warmer = faster. Cool the nerve and everything slows down.
Unmyelinated fibres use continuous conduction — every patch fires in turn, which is thorough but slow.
An express train skipping stations versus a local train stopping at every one: that is myelinated versus unmyelinated conduction.
Cold hands feel clumsy and numb because conduction genuinely slows in the cold.
Stub your toe and you feel two waves — a sharp instant pain (fast myelinated fibres) then a dull throb a moment later (slow unmyelinated fibres). Same injury, two different cables.

blocks.name: Three factors affecting conduction velocity
blocks.def: Fiber diameter, presence or absence of myelin, and temperature — all three independently speed up or slow down how fast an action potential travels.

blocks.name: Effect of fiber diameter on conduction velocity
blocks.def: Increasing axon radius increases conduction velocity, because internal resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area — a larger fiber has lower internal resistance, so current flows more easily. In unmyelinated axons specifically, conduction velocity is proportional to the SQUARE ROOT of axon diameter.

blocks.name: Effect of myelination on conduction velocity
blocks.def: Myelination has two key effects: it decreases the membrane's 'leakiness' to ions (making it hard for ions to escape except at the nodes of Ranvier), and it greatly reduces membrane capacitance (its ability to store charge), meaning little accumulated charge slows current flow within the axon. Together, these two effects dramatically speed up AP propagation in myelinated axons.

blocks.name: Effect of temperature on conduction velocity
blocks.def: Increasing temperature increases ion flow and speeds Na+ channel conductance kinetics, generally increasing conduction velocity (up to a point) — as temperature rises, the Na+/K+-ATPase also works faster. Conversely, cooled nerves conduct more slowly, since channels open and close more sluggishly at lower temperature.

blocks.name: Regular (continuous) conduction
blocks.def: The sequential spread of an action potential that occurs in UNmyelinated axons — action potentials are propagated continuously, as a moving wave.

blocks.name: <term d="Fast signalling in which the impulse jumps from one gap in the myelin sheath to the next.">Saltatory conduction</term>
blocks.def: The way action potentials are transmitted along MYELINATED nerve fibers. Depolarization occurs ONLY at the nodes of Ranvier, where membrane resistance is low; depolarization at one node is enough to raise the voltage at the next node to threshold. Action potentials don't propagate as a continuous wave — they recur at successive nodes and effectively 'hop' along the axon. This saves energy (fewer Na+/K+ pump cycles needed) and is considerably faster than regular conduction. ('Saltatory' comes from the Latin for 'leaping' — the signal leaps node to node.)

items: Absolute refractory period: for a short window the fibre cannot fire again no matter how strong the stimulus — the Na⁺ gates are inactivated.
Relative refractory period: it can fire, but only with a stronger-than-usual stimulus.
Refractory periods do two vital jobs: they cap the maximum firing rate, and they force the impulse to travel one way only (it cannot turn back into membrane that has just fired).

Sensory receptors are translators: they convert light, sound, pressure, heat or chemicals into electrical language — the only language the nervous system reads. That conversion is sensory transduction.
Each receptor has an adequate stimulus — the form of energy it is built for. This is why pressing on your closed eye produces a flash of light rather than a feeling of pressure.
By location: exteroceptors (outside world), interoceptors (internal organs), proprioceptors (body position).
Adaptation: with a constant, unchanging stimulus, receptors fire less and less. The nervous system cares about change, not sameness.
You stop feeling your watch, your ring or your shirt within minutes of dressing — textbook sensory adaptation. Now that you have read this, you can feel them again.
Walking into a kitchen and smelling food strongly, then barely noticing it ten minutes later — the food has not changed, your receptors have adapted.
Proprioception is why you can touch your nose with your eyes closed, and why you can climb stairs in the dark without looking at your feet.
This links straight across to Behavioural Science: habituation — learning to ignore a meaningless repeated stimulus, like the sound of a fan — is this same principle at the level of behaviour.

blocks.name: Refractory period (general)
blocks.def: The period during an action potential when the membrane's ability to respond to a second stimulus is markedly altered. It limits how many APs can be fired in a given time, and it's key in determining the DIRECTION of AP propagation (preventing the signal from doubling back on itself). Made up of two phases: absolute and relative.

blocks.x: ▶️Absolute and Relative Refractory PeriodVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Absolute refractory period
blocks.def: The period during which a second stimulus will NOT produce a second action potential, no matter how strong the stimulus is. Corresponds to the period when voltage-gated Na+ channels are open or in their inactivated state, and coincides with the entire duration of the action potential itself.

blocks.name: Relative refractory period
blocks.def: The period during which another action potential CAN be produced, but only with a stimulus stronger than the normal threshold (gradually decreasing back to threshold-level stimuli as time passes). Corresponds to the period when K+ channels are still open (a few milliseconds), roughly coinciding with the period of after-hyperpolarization.

blocks.name: Accommodation
blocks.def: The property of a nerve by which it adjusts to a SLOWLY increasing level of stimulus, so that its excitation threshold is never quite reached and no action potential is evoked — even though the resting potential creeps closer to threshold, it never quite gets there, because increased K+ conductance during the slow depolarization tends to repolarize the membrane at the same time, and the critical number of open Na+ channels needed to trigger an AP is never reached.

blocks.title: Change of subject — from firing to sensing

items: Everything above was about how a nerve fires. Everything below is about how the real world gets turned into firing.
The chain is: stimulus → receptor → pathway → brain area that interprets it.
Keep one idea in mind throughout: the nervous system only speaks one language — action potentials. Every sense must be translated into it.

blocks.name: Sensory physiology — the four components
blocks.def: Reception (the <term d="A protein that recognises and binds a specific signal molecule, triggering a response in the cell.">receptor</term> absorbs the stimulus's energy), transduction (conversion of that energy into a receptor/generator potential), transmission (receptor potentials are transmitted onward as action potentials to the CNS), and integration (processing of the frequency of incoming action potentials). Sensory information is fundamentally coded as the FREQUENCY of action potentials, not their size (since APs are all-or-none).

blocks.name: Sensory receptor (definition)
blocks.def: A structure that recognizes a stimulus in the internal or external environment. May be a free nerve ending, a specialized portion of a sensory neuron, a whole cell associated with a neuron ending, or a group of such cells. Sensory receptors convert environmental stimuli into membrane potentials through a process called sensory transduction.

blocks.name: Classification of sensory receptors by complexity
blocks.def: Simple receptors (associated with the 'general senses,' found throughout the body — as naked or encapsulated nerve endings) versus complex receptors (associated with the 'special senses,' found in only one or two specific body areas, using separate sensory cells or highly modified nerve endings — e.g., photoreceptors, olfactory receptors, hair cells, gustatory receptors).

blocks.name: Exteroceptors
blocks.def: Sensory receptors located at or near the skin surface, sensitive to stimuli occurring outside or on the surface of the body — touch, pain, temperature, vision, hearing, smell, and taste.

blocks.name: Interoceptors (visceroceptors)
blocks.def: Sensory receptors that respond to stimuli from visceral organs and blood vessels, associated with the autonomic nervous system — modulate sensations like pain, pressure, fatigue, hunger, thirst, and nausea.

blocks.name: Proprioceptors
blocks.def: Sensory receptors that respond to stimuli in skeletal muscles, tendons, ligaments, the inner ear, and joints — providing information about body position and movement.

blocks.title: Next up — two ways of sorting receptors

items: By location: exteroceptors (outside world), interoceptors (internal organs), proprioceptors (body position).
By stimulus type: mechano-, thermo-, photo-, chemo- and nociceptors — named simply after what they detect.
The names are transparent, so do not memorise them as a list: read the prefix and the answer is there.

blocks.name: Classification of sensory receptors by stimulus type
blocks.def: Mechanoreceptors (physical force — pressure/stretch), photoreceptors (light), thermoreceptors (temperature change), chemoreceptors (dissolved chemicals — taste, smell, or internal chemistry like O2/CO2/H+), nociceptors (pain), osmoreceptors (osmotic pressure change), and baroreceptors (pressure change).

blocks.name: Sensory transduction
blocks.def: The process by which sensory receptors convert environmental stimuli into electrical signals — interaction between the stimulus and receptor opens or closes ion channels, changing membrane potential in the form of a receptor or generator potential (which is a <term d="A small local change in membrane charge whose size depends on how strong the stimulus was.">graded potential</term>, and may be depolarizing or hyperpolarizing).

blocks.name: Adequate stimulus
blocks.def: The specific type of stimulus that a given receptor type is MOST sensitive to — e.g., light for cones, sound for hair cells.

blocks.title: Next up — why you stop noticing things

items: The nervous system is built to report change, not sameness. Constant news is no news.
Phasic receptors adapt fast (touch, smell) — they tell you something started.
Tonic receptors adapt slowly or not at all (pain, proprioception) — because that information must never be ignored.
That distinction is deliberate: you should stop feeling your shirt, but never stop feeling pain.

blocks.name: Adaptation (sensory)
blocks.def: A decrease in receptor responsiveness to a uniformly maintained stimulus of constant intensity, resulting in a decline in AP frequency over time and the stimulus feeling progressively weaker.

blocks.name: Phasic vs tonic receptors
blocks.def: Phasic receptors adapt QUICKLY (e.g., touch, odor, temperature, pressure — like the Pacinian corpuscle) — this is why you stop noticing your clothes touching your skin after a moment. Tonic receptors adapt SLOWLY (e.g., proprioceptors, blood pressure receptors, pain receptors) — this is why ongoing pain doesn't just fade away on its own.

blocks.name: Modality
blocks.def: Each distinct type of sensation we experience — pain, touch, pressure, etc. Modality is encoded by 'labeled lines,' meaning specific nerve fibers are dedicated to transmitting specific modalities, and which modality is perceived depends on WHERE in the CNS the relevant nerve tract terminates, not on any property of the signal itself.

blocks.name: Intensity coding
blocks.def: Stimulus intensity is coded in three ways: recruitment (how many sensory units are activated), the amplitude/frequency of action potentials fired by a sensory neuron, and activation of different types of receptors.

items: Afferent = Arrive, Efferent = Exit.
RMP ≈ −70 mV, and potassium sets it. If asked which ion dominates the resting potential, the answer is K⁺.
Faster = fatter, myelinated, warmer. Those are the only three factors.
Na⁺ in = depolarize; K⁺ out = repolarize. The whole action potential in one line.
Saltatory = to jump (same root as 'somersault').

blocks.title: Cleared up — the confusions that cost marks

items: All-or-none applies to a single fibre, not a whole nerve. A nerve as a whole gives graded responses because it contains many fibres.
Graded potentials summate; action potentials do not. That is exactly why both types exist.
Myelin does not conduct the impulse — it insulates so the impulse can skip ahead. Insulation, not wiring.
Stronger stimulus ≠ bigger action potential. It means more frequent spikes and more fibres recruited.
Absolute vs relative refractory: absolute = impossible at any strength; relative = possible, but needs a stronger stimulus.
← Body Fluids (Topic 01): the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients spent here were built and paid for there. No pump, no impulse.
← Homeostasis (Topic 02): sensory receptors are the sensors of countless control loops; this is the fast, electrical branch of that machinery.
→ Skeletal, Cardiac & Smooth Muscle (Topics 04–06): muscle is excitable tissue too. The same action potential you just learned is what triggers every contraction — including every heartbeat.
→ Communication Between Cells (Topic 07): the impulse reaching the terminal is where this topic stops and the synapse takes over.
The one-line summary: charge the membrane, reach threshold, fire all-or-none, propagate without fading — and code intensity by frequency, not size.

lines: Resting membrane potential, threshold, and the peak of the action potential — three numbers that anchor the whole curve.
Depolarisation is sodium rushing in; repolarisation is potassium leaving; the pump then restores the gradients, 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out for every 2 K<sup>+</sup> in.
During the absolute refractory period no stimulus of any strength fires a second action potential; during the relative period a stronger-than-normal one can.
Conduction velocity rises with myelination, because of saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier, and with fibre diameter.
